What Is the Gold Price?

The gold price refers to the current market value of gold, typically quoted per troy ounce in US dollars. It is one of the most widely watched financial benchmarks in the world, used by investors, central banks, jewelers, and manufacturers as a reference point for buying, selling, and valuing gold in all its forms.

What Is the Gold Price Today?

The gold price today refers to the current market value of gold traded globally in financial markets. Gold is usually priced per troy ounce in U.S. dollars, but many investors also track the value in other currencies. The price changes throughout the day as buyers and sellers trade gold through futures markets, bullion dealers, and financial exchanges. Factors such as inflation, interest rates, currency strength, and geopolitical events often influence daily movements. If you want to see a real-time update, you can check our latest gold price update which tracks the market as it changes.

Live Gold Price Chart

A live gold price chart allows investors to track how the price of gold moves throughout the day, week, or longer periods. Charts display price movements in real time and help identify trends, support levels, and potential price reversals. Many traders rely on charts to analyze short-term volatility and long-term market direction. Viewing historical data can also reveal how gold performs during inflation, economic uncertainty, or stock market downturns. You can explore different time ranges including daily and multi-year data using our interactive gold price chart to better understand market momentum.

Gold Price Per Ounce vs Per Gram

Gold is most commonly quoted per troy ounce in international markets, but many retail buyers and sellers prefer to measure gold per gram. One troy ounce equals approximately 31.1 grams, which means the gram price is simply the ounce price divided by this amount. Jewelers, coin dealers, and bullion buyers often use the gram price when calculating smaller purchases. Investors comparing bullion products should understand both measurements to evaluate value accurately. You can view the latest conversions and price comparisons on our gold price per gram guide which explains how these units relate.

Historical Gold Price Trends

Gold has a long history as a store of value and its price has experienced several major cycles over time. In periods of inflation, financial instability, or currency weakness, investors often turn to gold as a safe-haven asset. Historical charts show that gold experienced strong rallies during the 1970s inflation period, the 2008 financial crisis, and the global uncertainty surrounding the pandemic. Examining these trends helps investors understand how gold reacts during economic stress. For a deeper look at long-term movements, review our complete gold price history covering decades of market data.

Why Gold Prices Go Up and Down

Gold prices fluctuate due to a variety of economic and financial forces. Inflation expectations often push gold prices higher because investors seek protection against declining purchasing power. Interest rates also play a role; when rates rise, gold can become less attractive because it does not generate income. Currency strength, especially movements in the U.S. dollar, also affects the price since gold is priced globally in dollars. Geopolitical tensions and market uncertainty frequently drive demand for gold as a safe asset. Learn more about these drivers in our detailed gold price factors guide.

Gold Price Forecast

Gold price forecasts attempt to estimate future movements based on economic conditions, technical analysis, and market sentiment. Analysts evaluate factors such as inflation trends, central bank policy, global debt levels, and geopolitical risks when predicting gold’s future direction. Some forecasts suggest that gold may continue rising during periods of economic uncertainty or currency devaluation. However, predictions vary widely depending on market conditions and assumptions. Investors should always treat forecasts as possibilities rather than guarantees. You can explore different scenarios and expert opinions in our gold price prediction analysis.

Should You Buy Gold Right Now?

Whether it is a good time to buy gold depends on your investment goals, time horizon, and view of the global economy. Many investors purchase gold as a hedge against inflation, currency risk, or stock market volatility. Others add gold to diversify a broader investment portfolio. While gold can provide stability during economic uncertainty, its price can still experience periods of volatility. Evaluating current economic conditions and long-term financial plans is essential before buying. If you are considering an investment, our beginner’s guide to investing in gold explains common strategies.

Gold vs Silver Price Trends

Gold and silver are both precious metals widely used for investment and industrial purposes, but their price movements can differ significantly. Gold is often viewed as a long-term store of value and tends to move in response to macroeconomic trends such as inflation and currency shifts. Silver, on the other hand, has significant industrial demand in electronics and manufacturing, which can create different price patterns. Investors often compare the gold-to-silver ratio to evaluate relative value between the two metals. You can explore this relationship further in our gold vs silver comparison.

Where to Buy or Sell Gold

Gold can be bought and sold through several channels including bullion dealers, online marketplaces, banks, and local coin shops. Investors may choose to purchase gold coins, bars, or exchange-traded funds depending on their investment preferences. When selling gold, it is important to compare offers from multiple buyers to ensure a fair market price. Fees, premiums, and authentication processes can vary significantly between sellers and dealers. Understanding these factors can help maximize value during a transaction. Our guide to buying and selling gold explains how to choose reputable providers.

Gold Investment Strategies

Investing in gold can take many forms depending on an investor’s objectives and risk tolerance. Some investors prefer physical gold such as bullion bars or coins that can be stored privately or in secure vaults. Others gain exposure through financial products like gold exchange-traded funds, mining stocks, or futures contracts. Long-term investors often allocate a small percentage of their portfolio to gold as a hedge against economic instability. Diversification is typically the key principle when incorporating gold into a broader strategy. Learn more about portfolio approaches in our gold investment strategies guide.

What Factors Influence the Gold Price?

The gold price is shaped by a broad range of economic and geopolitical forces. Supply and demand play a foundational role, as do currency movements — particularly the strength of the US dollar, which tends to move inversely to gold. Inflation expectations, interest rates, central bank reserves, and global uncertainty all contribute to price fluctuations. When confidence in financial markets falls, demand for gold as a safe-haven asset typically rises, pushing the gold price higher.

Why Do People Track the Gold Price?

Gold has been used as a store of value for thousands of years, and its price remains a key indicator of broader economic sentiment. Investors monitor the gold price to hedge against inflation and currency risk, while industries such as jewelry, electronics, and dentistry track it to manage production costs. Whether you are considering gold as part of an investment portfolio or simply staying informed about global markets, understanding the gold price is a valuable part of financial literacy.

What Is the Gold Price Today?

The gold price today represents the current market value of gold, usually quoted per troy ounce in U.S. dollars. Investors, traders, and consumers monitor this price to make buying, selling, and investment decisions. Gold prices fluctuate constantly based on supply and demand, global economic conditions, and geopolitical events. Tracking the current gold price helps investors assess the market and plan their transactions. For up-to-date information, see the main Gold Price Today: Live Gold Price Chart and Market Trends pillar page.

Gold Price Per Ounce

Gold is commonly measured per troy ounce, which equals approximately 31.1 grams. This is the standard unit used in international trading, futures markets, and bullion sales. Investors buying large quantities of gold usually refer to the ounce price, as it reflects the global benchmark value. Understanding the price per ounce is essential for trading, comparing products, and evaluating investment performance. For a complete guide, visit the main Gold Price Today pillar page.

Gold Price Per Gram

Many retail buyers and jewelers prefer to track gold per gram because it is more practical for smaller purchases. The gram price is calculated by dividing the ounce price by 31.1 grams. This unit makes it easier to price coins, jewelry, and smaller bullion items accurately. Knowing both ounce and gram pricing helps investors and collectors compare deals and make informed decisions. Learn more about gold pricing on our Gold Price Today pillar page.

Factors Affecting Today's Gold Price

The daily gold price is influenced by several key factors, including inflation expectations, interest rates, currency movements, and geopolitical events. When markets are uncertain, gold often rises as investors seek a safe-haven asset. Conversely, strong economic growth or rising interest rates can reduce demand and lower the price. Monitoring these drivers can help you understand daily fluctuations and make smarter decisions. For broader trends, see our Gold Price Today pillar page.

How to Use This Information

Investors and buyers can use the current gold price per ounce or gram to time purchases, sales, or investments. Traders may use real-time data to capitalize on short-term market movements, while long-term investors consider price trends and forecasts. Understanding both the ounce and gram pricing allows you to compare products and evaluate opportunities. For a deeper overview and full market analysis, check the main Gold Price Today pillar page.

Understanding What Drives Gold Prices

Gold prices are influenced by a complex interplay of economic, geopolitical, and market factors. Understanding these drivers can help you make informed decisions about buying or selling gold.

Inflation and Interest Rates

Gold has historically been viewed as an inflation hedge. When inflation rises or interest rates fall, investors often turn to gold as a store of value, driving up prices. Conversely, when inflation is controlled or interest rates rise, gold may become less attractive.

Currency Movements

Gold is priced in US dollars. When the dollar weakens, gold becomes cheaper for international buyers, increasing demand and pushing prices up. A strong dollar typically puts downward pressure on gold prices.

Global Demand and Supply

Jewelry demand, particularly from China and India, significantly impacts gold prices. Central bank purchases and mining production also affect supply. When demand exceeds supply, prices tend to rise.

Geopolitical Uncertainty

During times of political instability or economic uncertainty, investors flock to gold as a safe-haven asset. Events like wars, political crises, and financial market volatility often trigger price increases.

Gold Price Per Gram Explained

The gold price per gram is a common measurement used for calculating the value of gold jewelry, small gold items, and investment pieces. Understanding how this price is calculated helps you make better purchasing and selling decisions.

How Gold Price Per Gram Is Calculated

Gold prices are typically quoted per troy ounce in international markets. To convert to per gram, divide the spot price by 31.1035 (the number of grams in a troy ounce). The final price depends on the purity of the gold.

The Role of Purity

Gold purity is measured in karats. 24K gold is pure (99.9%), while 18K is 75% gold, and 14K is 58.3% gold. The price per gram decreases proportionally with lower purity levels.

Factors Affecting Gram Price

Beyond spot price and purity, premiums charged by dealers, manufacturing costs, and market demand all influence the final price per gram you pay or receive.

A Beginner's Guide to Investing in Gold

Gold has been a valuable commodity for thousands of years and remains a popular investment choice today. This guide covers the main ways to invest in gold and the factors to consider.

Ways to Invest in Gold

Physical Gold: Buy gold bars, coins, or jewelry. Requires secure storage and insurance.

Gold ETFs: Exchange-traded funds that track gold prices, offering easy trading and no physical storage needs.

Gold Mining Stocks: Invest in companies that mine gold. Offers leverage to gold prices but carries additional company-specific risks.

Gold Futures: Contracts to buy or sell gold at a future date. More advanced and carries higher risk.

Benefits of Gold Investment

Gold provides portfolio diversification, acts as an inflation hedge, and serves as a safe-haven during economic uncertainty. It has historically maintained value over long periods.

How to Sell Gold for the Best Price

Whether you have gold jewelry, coins, bars, or scrap gold, selling strategically can significantly impact how much you receive. Here's how to maximize your returns.

Determine Your Gold's Value

First, determine the purity (karat) and weight of your gold. Current gold price multiplied by the purity percentage gives you the intrinsic gold value. Dealers typically pay a percentage of this value.

Where to Sell Gold

Local Jewelers: Convenient but may offer lower prices.

Pawn Shops: Quick cash but often the lowest offers.

Online Dealers: Competitive prices, especially for coins and bars.

Auction Sites: Potential for higher prices but takes longer and has fees.

Tips for Getting the Best Price

Get multiple quotes from different buyers. Understand the current spot price. Consider the condition and rarity of jewelry. Time your sale when gold prices are favorable.

Gold vs Silver: Comparing Precious Metals

Both gold and silver are precious metals with investment appeal, but they have distinct characteristics. Understanding the differences helps you decide which is better suited for your portfolio.

Price and Volatility

Gold trades at much higher prices (over $2,000 per ounce) compared to silver (around $25-30 per ounce). Silver is more volatile, with larger percentage swings both up and down.

Industrial Demand

Silver has significant industrial uses in electronics, solar panels, and medical applications. Gold is primarily used in jewelry and as a monetary asset. Industrial demand affects silver prices more directly.

Portfolio Role

Gold is often seen as a store of value and safe-haven asset. Silver is sometimes called "poor man's gold" and can offer more upside potential but with higher risk.

Which Is Better?

The choice depends on your investment goals, risk tolerance, and portfolio needs. Many investors choose to hold both for diversification.

Proven Gold Investment Strategies

There are several established strategies for incorporating gold into your investment portfolio. Each approach has its own risk-reward profile and time horizon.

Long-Term Holding

Buy and hold gold for years or decades. This strategy relies on gold's historical ability to preserve value and hedge against inflation. It requires patience but minimal active management.

Portfolio Hedging

Use gold to hedge against market downturns and currency devaluation. A small allocation (5-10%) to gold can reduce portfolio volatility and provide insurance against economic crises.

Dollar-Cost Averaging

Invest a fixed amount regularly (monthly or quarterly) regardless of price. This approach smooths out price volatility and removes the stress of timing the market.

Diversification with Precious Metals

Combine gold with other precious metals like silver, platinum, and palladium. Each metal has unique drivers and can provide complementary diversification benefits.

What is the best gold stock?

There's no single "best" gold stock — it depends on your risk tolerance and investment goals. Large-cap miners like Newmont and Barrick Gold offer stability and dividends, while junior miners carry higher risk with greater upside potential. Always review financials, reserve grades, and geopolitical exposure before investing.

What if I invested $10,000 in gold 20 years ago?

A $10,000 investment in gold around 2004 would be worth approximately $60,000–$70,000 today, reflecting gold's long-term appreciation as a store of value. Gold mining stocks have shown even wider variance — some have significantly outperformed the metal itself, others have not.

What is the best Canadian gold stock?

Canada is home to some of the world's largest gold producers. Agnico Eagle, Barrick Gold, and Kinross Gold are among the most widely held Canadian gold stocks, listed on the TSX. Each differs in asset geography, production scale, and dividend policy.

Which gold company did Warren Buffett buy?

In 2020, Berkshire Hathaway purchased a stake in Barrick Gold — a notable move given Buffett's long-standing skepticism of gold as an asset. Berkshire later sold most of the position, but the investment drew widespread attention to gold equities.

Investing in Gold Stocks

Gold stocks offer investors leveraged exposure to the gold price — when gold rises, miners' profits can rise faster, amplifying returns compared to holding physical gold. Many established producers also pay dividends, making them a popular choice for investors seeking both growth potential and income.

Silver stocks offer investors leveraged exposure to the silver price — when silver rises, miners' profits can rise faster, amplifying returns compared to holding physical gold. Many established producers also pay dividends, making them a popular choice for investors seeking both growth potential and income.

Which silver stock is best?

The top silver stocks depend on your investment style. Pan American Silver, First Majestic Silver, and Wheaton Precious Metals are among the most widely held, offering a mix of production scale, geographic diversification, and financial stability. Streaming companies like Wheaton tend to carry lower operational risk than pure miners.

What is the main stock for silver?

Wheaton Precious Metals (WPM) is often considered the benchmark silver stock due to its size, liquidity, and unique streaming business model. First Majestic Silver (AG) is another closely watched name for investors wanting direct exposure to silver mining operations.

What's the best silver stock to buy in Canada?

Several top silver companies are headquartered in Canada and trade on the TSX. Wheaton Precious Metals, Pan American Silver, and First Majestic Silver are among the most prominent Canadian-listed options, offering varying risk profiles from conservative streamers to active primary silver miners.

What did Elon Musk say about silver?

Musk has commented on silver primarily in the context of industrial demand — noting its critical role in solar panels and electronics. While not a direct endorsement of silver stocks, his remarks on the metal's importance to the energy transition have drawn renewed investor attention to silver's supply outlook.

Energy stocks offer investors exposure to oil, gas, pipelines, and renewables — with many established producers and midstream companies paying substantial dividends. Canadian energy equities in particular are known for strong cash flows and shareholder returns, making them a core holding in many income-focused portfolios.

What is the best energy stock to invest in today?

The best energy stock depends on your outlook for oil prices and your income vs. growth preference. Integrated majors like Canadian Natural Resources offer stability and dividends, while smaller producers carry more commodity price sensitivity. Pipeline companies like Enbridge provide bond-like income with regulated revenue streams.

Which Canadian energy stock is best to buy?

Canadian Natural Resources (CNQ), Suncor Energy, and Cenovus are among the most widely held Canadian energy stocks, known for large reserve bases and consistent dividends. For pipeline exposure, Enbridge and TC Energy are the dominant names on the TSX.

What energy stock did Buffett buy?

Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway has been a major buyer of Occidental Petroleum, accumulating a significant stake over several years. Berkshire also owns Berkshire Hathaway Energy, giving it substantial exposure to utilities and energy infrastructure alongside its equity positions.

What are the best energy stocks in Canada 2026?

Heading into 2026, Canadian Natural Resources, Suncor, and Tourmaline Oil remain top picks among analysts for their strong balance sheets and shareholder return programs. Enbridge continues to be a go-to for dividend investors, while emerging LNG-linked plays are attracting attention as global natural gas demand grows.

Is there a silver ETF in Canada?

Yes — Canadian investors can access silver through ETFs listed on the TSX, including the Sprott Physical Silver Trust (PSLV), which holds allocated physical silver and is structured as a closed-end fund. It's a widely used vehicle for Canadians seeking direct silver exposure with favourable tax treatment.

Is silver ETF risky?

Silver ETFs carry more volatility than gold ETFs, as silver is sensitive to both investor sentiment and industrial demand cycles. Price swings of 20–30% in a year are not uncommon. Physical silver ETFs are generally lower risk than silver miner ETFs, which amplify moves in the underlying metal.

What is Warren Buffett's favorite ETF?

Buffett has long recommended low-cost S&P 500 index funds for most investors, specifically citing the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO) and similar funds as the best long-term vehicle for the average investor. He has not publicly endorsed any silver or precious metals ETF.

Is tungsten a good investment?

Tungsten has strong fundamentals as an investment theme in 2026. China's export restrictions have created a supply gap that Western producers cannot quickly fill, putting upward pressure on APT and concentrate prices. As a critical mineral with no easy substitute in many applications, tungsten is increasingly appearing on government strategic mineral lists in the US, EU, and Canada — which typically drives both price appreciation and investment into domestic producers.

Is tungsten on the stock market?

There are no tungsten futures contracts, making direct price exposure difficult. The primary way to invest in tungsten is through publicly traded mining companies listed on exchanges like the TSX and ASX. Unlike gold or silver, tungsten has no ETF — meaning individual stock selection is the main route for investors seeking exposure to the metal.

What company mines tungsten in Canada?

Almonty Industries (TSX: AII) is the most prominent tungsten company with Canadian roots, operating mines across Spain, Portugal, and South Korea. Canada's Cantung mine in the Northwest Territories — once one of the world's highest-grade tungsten deposits — has historically been a significant producer, though it has seen limited activity in recent years due to price cycles.

What companies produce tungsten?

China dominates global tungsten production through state-controlled operations, accounting for roughly 80% of world supply. Outside China, the key publicly traded producers include Almonty Industries, W Resources (LSE: WRES), and Vital Metals. Global Tungsten & Powders, a subsidiary of Plansee Group, is a major processor though it trades privately. As Western nations push to reduce reliance on Chinese supply, junior miners with tungsten assets in politically stable jurisdictions are drawing increasing investor and government interest.

Tungsten stocks offer investors exposure to one of the world's most strategically critical metals — used in defense, semiconductors, and industrial tooling. With China controlling the majority of global supply and tightening export quotas in 2026, Western tungsten producers are attracting serious investor attention as governments and industries scramble to secure alternative sources.

Mining and commodity investing covers far more than just gold and silver. Global financial markets include publicly traded companies and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) focused on dozens of metals used in manufacturing, technology, energy, and infrastructure.

These metals fall into several major categories including precious metals, base metals, battery materials, rare earth elements, nuclear metals, and strategic technology metals.

This guide provides a comprehensive overview of metals that have dedicated mining companies, commodity markets, or ETF exposure.

Precious Metals

Precious metals are historically used as stores of value and investment assets. They also have significant industrial uses in electronics, medicine, and catalysis.

Major precious metals with mining sectors:

  • Gold
  • Silver
  • Platinum
  • Palladium

Gold and silver have the largest investment markets, including physical ETFs and mining company ETFs. Platinum and palladium are heavily used in automotive catalytic converters and hydrogen technologies.

Reference: Investopedia

Platinum Group Metals (PGMs)

Platinum group metals are rare elements typically mined together in the same geological deposits. These metals are essential for catalytic converters, fuel cells, and chemical processing.

Platinum group metals include:

  • Platinum
  • Palladium
  • Rhodium
  • Iridium
  • Ruthenium
  • Osmium

Most global PGM production occurs in South Africa and Russia. Learn more about PGM stocks and platinum ETFs.

Reference: USGS

Base and Industrial Metals

Base metals are widely used in construction, transportation, electrical infrastructure, and manufacturing. These metals form the backbone of global industrial production.

Major base metals with mining sectors:

  • Copper — Stocks | ETFs
  • Aluminum — Stocks
  • Nickel — ETFs
  • Zinc
  • Lead
  • Tin
  • Iron
  • Chromium
  • Molybdenum

Copper and iron ore represent some of the largest mining markets in the world.

Reference: World Bank

Battery and Energy Transition Metals

The electrification of transportation and renewable energy systems has dramatically increased demand for certain metals used in batteries and energy storage technologies.

Key battery and energy metals include:

  • Lithium — ETFs
  • Nickel — ETFs
  • Cobalt
  • Graphite
  • Manganese
  • Vanadium

These metals are critical components of lithium-ion batteries used in electric vehicles and grid storage.

Reference: IEA

Nuclear Energy Metals

Certain metals are mined specifically for nuclear energy production.

Nuclear fuel metals include:

  • Uranium — ETFs
  • Thorium

Uranium mining supports the global nuclear power industry, while thorium is being researched as an alternative nuclear fuel.

Reference: World Nuclear Association

Rare earth elements consist of 17 chemically similar metals used in magnets, electronics, lasers, and advanced defense systems. These materials are essential for wind turbines, electric vehicles, and high-performance electronics.

  • Neodymium

  • Holmium

Strategic and Critical Metals

Strategic metals are considered essential for modern industry but often have limited global supply or geopolitical risks. Many governments classify these materials as "critical minerals."

Examples include:

  • Tungsten
  • Antimony
  • Niobium
  • Tantalum
  • Zirconium
  • Hafnium
  • Beryllium
  • Bismuth

These metals are used in aerospace alloys, electronics, defense technologies, and high-temperature materials. See our critical minerals stocks and ETFs.

Reference: USGS

Technology and Semiconductor Metals

Several metals play specialized roles in electronics, semiconductors, solar panels, and telecommunications. These metals are often produced as by-products of larger mining operations.

Technology metals include:

  • Gallium
  • Germanium
  • Indium
  • Tellurium
  • Selenium
  • Cadmium
  • Rhenium

They are used in solar cells, fiber optics, semiconductors, and aerospace alloys.

Reference: IEA
